title: How Safe Are Hospitals? The Hidden Risk of Infection
text:
When we go to hospital, we expect to leave healthier than when we arrived. But what if the place we go to recover can also expose us to another health risk?



Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are infections that patients pick up during medical care, such as infections of surgical wounds, the urinary tract or the lungs. They vary in type and severity, and they can increase the risk of illness, death and healthcare costs. Anyone who goes to hospital, including us or someone close to us, could be affected.






A 2019 study estimated that Germany had around 478,000 cases of five common HAIs, causing about 16,000 deaths. These numbers sound alarming, but they do not tell us what to expect as a patient. This raises a question:

How likely are you to catch an infection in a German hospital, and how serious is it, compared with the rest of Europe?


How the health impact was measured
A study by Zacher et al. (2019) measured the harm caused by five common types of hospital infection in Germany in 2011. These were urinary tract infection (UTI), pneumonia (HAP), bloodstream infection (BSI), surgical site infection (SSI) and Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI). The study estimated how many people developed these infections, how many deaths they caused, and how much healthy life was lost.
The estimates are based on a survey of hospital patients across Europe in 2011 and 2012, run by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. The researchers developed a new method, adapted from an approach originally used for Europe as a whole. It works for both large and small samples, so it can be applied to a single country such as Germany (Zacher 2019).
To compare the infections, the researchers used a measure called the Disability-Adjusted Life Year (DALY). One DALY represents one year of healthy life lost, either through dying earlier than expected or through living with illness or disability. As it combines both, it allows very different infections to be compared on a single scale.

Deaths and DALYs show different sides of the same problem. We begin with infections and deaths, which are easy to picture. Table 1 sets out the estimated yearly numbers of infections and deaths for Germany. The last column, share leading to death, is our own calculation. It divides the number of deaths by the number of infections to show what proportion of infections were estimated to end in death.
UTI was by far the most common infection, with over 214,000 cases in 2011, about twice as many as HAP in second place. HAP had around 107,000 cases, and although only 3.7% of them ended in death, that still added up to about 3,970 deaths, among the highest of the five. BSI was the rarest, at around 27,000 cases, yet roughly 14.5% of them ended in death, the highest share of the five. In contrast, UTI, despite having the most cases, had the lowest share, at only 1.7%.
So how likely is an infection, and how serious? It depends on the type. UTI was the most common but the least likely to end in death, while the much rarer BSI was the most likely to end in death. These are estimates, but the gap between the two is wide enough to be clear. The takeaway is that how often an infection occurs is not enough to tell us how dangerous it is. How common an infection is and how severe it is need to be weighed together. DALYs do this in a single measure, which allows us to compare Germany with the rest of Europe.


How does Germany compare with Europe?








Figure 1: Healthy years of life lost (DALYs) per 100,000 people by type of infection, Germany and the EU/EEA average, 2011-2012. Source: Zacher et al. (2019).




To see how Germany compares with the rest of Europe, Figure 1 shows the healthy years of life lost (DALYs) per 100,000 people for each type of infection, for Germany and the EU/EEA average, which is the average across the European countries in the survey. Using rates per 100,000 people lets countries of different sizes be compared fairly. The thin lines show the likely range, meaning the range the true value probably falls in, because these figures are estimates and carry some uncertainty.
Across all five infections combined, the study estimates 308.2 DALYs per 100,000 people for Germany (likely range 221 to 416) and 290.0 for the EU/EEA average (likely range 215 to 377) (Zacher et al. 2019). Germany’s figure is about 6% higher, which points to a higher health burden from these infections, meaning more healthy years lost. The two ranges overlap, which means the real gap could be larger or smaller than this. These totals combine all five infections. As each figure is an estimate, the bars in Figure 1 do not exactly add up to the totals.
Not all five infections contribute equally to Germany’s higher total. UTI and CDI contribute the most, with Germany’s figure above the EU/EEA average by about 25 DALYs per 100,000 people for UTI and about 16 for CDI. HAP shows the opposite pattern, with Germany about 24 DALYs per 100,000 people lower. BSI makes up a large share of the health lost in Germany, but the EU/EEA figure is similar, and SSI is almost identical as well, so neither contributes much to Germany’s higher total. Two infections, UTI and CDI, therefore account for the difference in the total.
Another way to compare the countries is how likely it is that a hospital patient has an infection, which is what prevalence measures. This is the share of hospital patients who have an infection on the day of the survey. In Germany, about 5.0% of patients had an infection, compared with about 5.7% across the EU/EEA (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control 2013). These figures cover infections of any type, not only the five in the study, giving a broader picture of infections in hospital. The researchers describe Germany’s prevalence as relatively low compared with the EU/EEA (Zacher et al. 2019).
At first glance, these two results seem to conflict. Both can be true because prevalence looks only at patients in hospital, while DALYs count the healthy years lost across the whole population. A country can have a smaller share of infected patients and still lose more healthy years if more people spend time in hospital. The researchers suggest this may be the case in Germany, which has a large number of hospital beds (Zacher et al. 2019). So compared with the rest of Europe, Germany loses slightly more healthy years than the EU/EEA average, even though a slightly smaller share of its hospital patients are infected.


So, what does this mean for us?
We started by asking how likely we are to catch an infection in a German hospital, how serious it is, and how Germany compares with the rest of Europe. The first two answers depend on the type of infection. UTI was the most common but the least likely to end in death, while BSI was much rarer but the most likely. How common an infection is and how severe it is need to be weighed together, which is what DALYs do.
As for how Germany compares with the rest of Europe, it had slightly higher DALYs per 100,000 people than the EU/EEA average, about 308 against 290. This points to a higher health burden, meaning more healthy years lost, even though a slightly smaller share of hospital patients in Germany had an infection, about 5.0% against 5.7% for the EU/EEA. This may be partly explained by Germany’s large number of hospital beds, which can mean more people being admitted to hospital, even when a stay could be avoided, and therefore more chances of picking up an infection (Zacher et al. 2019).
So what can be done? Reducing avoidable hospital stays, together with a stronger focus on hygiene measures and infection prevention and control, are important steps towards reducing the healthy years lost to these infections (Zacher et al. 2019). These steps can involve everyone who comes into contact with hospitals, from the healthcare system and staff to patients and visitors like us.

Whenever we or someone close to us goes to hospital, a good place to start is knowing that hospital infections carry different levels of risk, and what can help reduce it.

text: I am Thunchanok, a Master of Business Analytics student at Monash University with a background in accounting. I have a strong interest in data visualisation, data analysis, and storytelling. I enjoy exploring data to find interesting patterns and turning them into clear and engaging stories. This blog is a collection of my data stories and visualisation projects created during my studies. I hope you enjoy reading them as much as I enjoyed creating them!
